turns.speaker: A
turns.text: There's one part of a German watch that collectors always look at first. It's a small bridge near the balance wheel, isn't it?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Yes, it's called the balance cock. It holds the top of the balance wheel in place. In Glashütte watches, it's often covered with a hand-engraved pattern of leaves and flowers.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Absolutely. The engraver works under a microscope or a strong magnifying glass. The main tool is called a burin. It's a small steel tool with a very sharp point that cuts tiny lines into the metal.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: There's a general design, but the cutting is done freehand. That means there's no machine guiding the tool. The engraver controls every line with their own hand.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So no two are exactly the same.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's the beauty of it. If you put two balance cocks side by side, you'll see small differences. Some people say they can even recognize which engraver made a piece, just by the style.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Isn't it a little strange to put so much work into a part most people never see?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Maybe. But many owners turn the watch over and look through the case back every day. For them, that tiny engraved bridge is the signature of the watch. It shows a human being was there.
